selection.revision: Prompt: Explain how a rise in a country's interest rate can lead to appreciation of its currency. Answer: Higher interest rates attract foreign investors and savers (1); they must buy the currency, so demand and its value rise, other things equal (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Hedge-only emphasis ('do not guarantee') omits the mechanism examined in 2021 P1 Q13 (higher interest: foreign investors buy the currency, appreciation; ER: learners gave effects on exports instead).

selection.revision: Prompt: The exchange rate changes from US$1 = N$18 to US$1 = N$20. A Namibian firm imports goods costing US$100. (a) Calculate the cost in N$ before and after (b) State whether the Namibia dollar has appreciated or depreciated against the US dollar. Answer: N$1,800 and N$2,000 (1); depreciated (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Calculation verified (100x18=1,800; 100x20=2,000; +200; N$ depreciates vs US$). Closest to 2024 P1 Q17 conversion skill. Language 'third-currency quotation' and peg wording too heavy for ESL; peg claim is Namibian/time-sensitive.

selection.revision: Marking: produces more of a good, or the same output with fewer resources, than another producer (1); using the same amount of resources (1). Tariff 2.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Correct (ER 2021: more output with the same resources) but 1 mark for a two-part definition; exam definition is 2 marks. V lacks a standalone card, so keep.

selection.revision: Marking: producing a good at a lower opportunity cost (1); than another producer / relative to another (1). Tariff 2.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Matches 2023 P1 Q19 (ER: learners defined absolute advantage instead) but 1 mark for 'lower opportunity cost' while the exam scheme gives 2.

selection.revision: Prompt: With the same resources, A can make 30 cloth or 15 grain and B can make 12 cloth or 12 grain. Explain who has the absolute advantage. Answer: A makes 18 more cloth and 3 more grain (2), so A has absolute advantage in both (1); the figures show output if all resources go to one good, not both together (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Differences verified (18 and 3). 'alternative maxima' is jargon for ESL.

selection.revision: Prompt: X makes 100 units in 10 labour hours; Y makes 150 units in 30 hours. Who has the absolute advantage? Explain. Answer: X = 100/10 = 10 units per hour; Y = 150/30 = 5 per hour (1); X is more productive although Y's total is larger, because Y used three times the hours (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Right misconception (unequal inputs) but no numbers; 100/10 vs 150/30 gives 10 vs 5 per hour, which the card never shows.

selection.revision: Prompt: With the same resources, A can make 30 cloth or 15 grain and B can make 12 cloth or 12 grain. Calculate the opportunity cost of one grain for A and for B. Answer: A = 30/15 = 2 cloth (1); B = 12/12 = 1 cloth (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Cleanest calculation card (both producers' opportunity cost); uses a second dataset (12/6, 4/4) and jargon ('equal-resource one-period maxima'). Change to the data used by V:P03 and V:007.

selection.revision: Marking: B (1) because it gives up 1 cloth per grain, less than A's 2 (1). Tariff 2.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: A one-line deduction (B 1 < A 2) carries 4 marks (1+1+2) while the explanation repeats the evidence.

selection.revision: Prompt: Explain why a producer with an absolute advantage in both goods cannot also have a comparative advantage in both. Answer: The opportunity cost of one good is the inverse of the other's (1); if A's cost of cloth is lower, B's cost of grain must be lower (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: 'not automatically the comparative-advantage producer of both' understates the point: with two goods and two producers one producer cannot have comparative advantage in both (unless costs are equal).

selection.revision: Prompt: A can make 30 cloth or 15 grain and B can make 12 cloth or 12 grain with the same resources. A pupil says B cannot gain from trade because A is better at both. Explain the error. Answer: B gives up 1 cloth per grain but A gives up 2 (1); a trade price between 1 and 2 cloth per grain benefits both (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Valuable error ('B cannot gain because A is better at both'); revise to V data and plain language.

selection.revision: Marking: for up to 3; against up to 3; judgement with stated condition up to 3 (total 9).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Effects of depreciation on the current account are 2.3/3.3-adjacent (not the 7.4 bullet on causes of fluctuation) but within 'effects on BoP'; judgement 1 of 9 marks under-rewards evaluation.

selection.revision: Prompt: Define a developed country. Answer: a country with high GDP per head (1) and high living standards, e.g. long life expectancy and high productivity (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Exam asks 'define a developed country' (2024 P1 Q19: high GDP per head plus another characteristic, 2 marks); prompt 'using more than a sector label' is unclear.

selection.revision: Prompt: Describe two characteristics of a developing country. Answer: any two of low GDP per head, high birth rate/fast population growth, high death rate/low life expectancy, high unemployment, reliance on primary products (1 each).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Hedged definition; exam asks to discuss characteristics of a developing country (2024 P2 Q2(c), 7 marks; ER: learners only listed).

selection.revision: Prompt: Explain how poor transport and a lack of skills can keep a developing country at a low stage of development. Answer: poor roads delay inputs and raise costs of reaching markets (2); unskilled workers cannot use machines well, so output per worker and incomes stay low (2).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Reasons for slower development (poor transport, skills) are valid but the prompt is heavy and the first mark credits the stem ('transport/training improved').

selection.revision: Marking: growth in the share of the population living in towns and cities (1); because of movement of people from rural to urban areas (1). Accept either wording.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Marking requires 'proportion rather than number', which would deny a mark to the common textbook definition 'movement of people from rural areas to towns and cities' (2020 P2 Q6(a), 2021 P1 Q22).

selection.revision: Prompt: A district has 10,000 people. In one year: births 300, deaths 100, immigrants 80, emigrants 120. Calculate (a) natural increase, (b) net migration, (c) total change and the population growth rate. Answer: 200 (1); -40 (1); +160, 1.6% (1). Tariff 3.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Verified: natural +200, net -40, total +160, final 10,160, +1.6%. It is a calculation, and the first marking point credits stem facts.

selection.revision: Marking: total growth = natural increase + net migration (1); two countries can have equal growth from different births, deaths or migration (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Sound transfer (same total growth, different causes); marking credits the stem.

selection.revision: Answer: The average number of children a woman would have in her lifetime if current birth rates for each age group continued. Marking: average children per woman (1); over her lifetime at current age-specific rates (1).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Accurate (TFR) but 'hypothetical woman' is heavy for ESL and marking text is a placeholder.

selection.revision: Marking: immigrants minus emigrants (1); over a stated period, usually a year (1). Rate: accept 'per 1,000 population'.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Matches 2023 P1 Q21 scheme (difference between immigrants and emigrants over the year, 2 marks) but marking is placeholder text and the denominator remark is a rate point.

selection.revision: Prompt: Give two reasons why a country with a low crude death rate may not have better health services. Answer: any two of young population, fewer deaths from disease at present, accidents/conflict, inaccurate data (1 each).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Age structure plus 'health conditions' is a narrow, partly circular pair; fair alternatives (disease burden, HIV, conflict) are not accepted.

selection.revision: Marking: accept any two of GDP/real income per head, life expectancy, literacy/education, infant mortality, access to health services, HDI.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Marking accepts only real income per person and service access; life expectancy, literacy, infant mortality and HDI are equally valid (cf. 2023 P1 Q22, 2024 P1 Q18).

selection.revision: Prompt: Explain how a larger working-age population could increase an economy's output. Answer: more workers can produce more goods and services (1) if they have jobs, skills and equipment; also a bigger market and more taxpayers (1). Tariff 2.
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Prompt lists the conditions (skills, jobs, equipment, services), so the answer restates it.

selection.revision: Marking (b) 7: transport/training mechanism 3; total change +160 and final population 10,160 2; link of demographic change to capacity 2 (200 and -40 credited once, in (a)).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Verified (200, -40, +160, 10,160). Double-credits the same figures in (a) and (b) (200 and -40 appear in both marking lists).

selection.revision: (d) Discuss whether the new factory jobs will improve living conditions in the region (7).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Part (d) asks whether 'population growth alone proves improved living conditions', a claim the stem never makes; the real question is whether the new jobs improve conditions.

selection.revision: Marking: for up to 3; against up to 3; judgement with stated condition up to 3 (total 9).
selection.why: Selected after the stated revision: Sound (working-age share is potential not gain); judgement 1 of 9 marks under-rewards evaluation.

selection.revision: ANSWER: Any one of: life expectancy (health/survival), education or literacy, housing, access to sanitation/clean water (1).
MARKING: Income adjusted for price changes / real income (1); divided by population (1).
ANSWER: The average number of years a newborn baby is expected to live (1) if current death rates stay the same (1).
ANSWER: Income per head shows the average money resources per person (1); sanitation access shows how many people actually have a service, so a high average income does not guarantee access (1).
PROMPT: An economy has real GDP of N$120 million and 10,000 people. Calculate real GDP per person (2).
PROMPT: A learner says 'Disposable income is real income because tax has been taken off.' Explain why this is wrong (2).
PROMPT: Total real income rises 10% and population rises 20%. What happens to real income per person, and why? ANSWER: It falls (about 8%) because population grows faster than income (1+1).

PROMPT: Two districts have the same real GDP per person. In A income is concentrated and water access is limited. In B income is widely shared and water access is reliable. Explain why equal GDP per person does not mean equal living standards (4).

ANSWER: Within a country, regions/groups differ in access to jobs, skills, assets and services (1). Between countries, capital, infrastructure, skills and institutions differ, and a country average can hide differences inside each country (1).
MARKING: Average income hides unequal distribution or local barriers (1); so some residents do not get meaningful access to the service (1). Accept remoteness, cost, quality as local barriers.
PROMPT: Explain how unequal access to training and transport can contribute to income disparities within a country (4).

ANSWER: Learners reach materials without the long journey, saving time and cost (mechanism); better skills or qualifications can improve job chances and income if the learner can use the materials and support is available (consequence).
MARKING: Some residents lack affordable devices, connectivity or skills (1); so a service that is online-only excludes them and access becomes uneven (1).

MARKING (2 each): (a) income adjusted for prices (1) divided by population (1). (b) average years a newborn is expected to live (1) if current death rates continue (1). (c) same mean can hide very different distributions (1) so some people get far less than average (1). (d) enrolment counts attendance (1) but not what is learned (1). (e) coverage counts those with a service (1) reliability is whether it works consistently (1). (f) unequal access to or ability to use IT (1) because of cost, skills or connectivity (1). (g) regions/groups differ in access to jobs, training or transport (1) so opportunities and incomes differ (1). (h) one indicator shows only one dimension (1) several give a fuller picture (1).
MARKING: in (a) replace 'N$12,000 detail' with 'both districts have the same population (10,000)'; keep N$12,000 credit only in (b).

PROMPT: Evaluate whether a high national real income per head shows that most people in a country have high living standards (8). MARKING: for (up to 3), against: distribution and non-income dimensions (up to 3), judgement with a stated condition (2).

requirements.syllabus_text: describe the nature of the economic problem (limited resources and unlimited wants)
requirements.demand: Recall and understand: state and explain scarcity; distinguish scarcity from shortage/surplus/income.
requirements.adequate_response: Names limited resources AND unlimited wants and the resulting need to choose; applies to a given constraint.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q1 outline scarcity [1]; 2021 P1 Q1 'limited resources and unlimited wants' = scarcity [2] (well answered); 2022 P1 Q1 term for finite resources/unlimited wants (well answered); 2024 P1 Q1 why choices must be made (scarcity/unlimited wants or OC) (well answered). No misconception recorded in ERs.
requirements.repetition: Both banks carry the shortage/surplus-vs-scarcity misconception (V-010, J-007); acceptable pair of opposite directions.
requirements.why: V definition names unlimited wants and the consequence; J-001 omits 'unlimited'; J-002 repeats it.

requirements.syllabus_text: explain and illustrate opportunity cost
requirements.demand: Understand/apply: define with 'next-best', identify the OC in a case, recognise free options have OC, illustrate (diagram).
requirements.adequate_response: Whole definition including NEXT best alternative; picks the correct alternative from a case; does not add all alternatives; for diagrams, reads OC from a movement along the curve.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P2 Q4(c) define OC + explain example in extract [4] (ER: majority 2 marks for example, lost definition marks; some used own example not the extract); 2022 P2 (b) 7 marks (ER: key word NEXT missing; could not extract best alternative); 2023 P1 Q1 [3] police vs rural development (well answered: sacrifice next best alternative). No PPC question found in 2020-2024 texts.
requirements.gap: No extract-based 'define OC and explain an example from the extract' item (2020 P2 Q4(c)); no government-spending OC item (2022 P2, 2023 P1).
requirements.repetition: V-005/V-006/J-004 all give a single learner/team example; V-P02 and J-P01 repeat them.
requirements.why: V covers definition, free-option OC, numeric discrimination and a checked PPC; add J-003 (all-options misconception).

requirements.syllabus_text: evaluate the implications of specific courses of action in terms of opportunity cost
requirements.demand: Evaluate: weigh benefits gained against the OC for a stated objective and reach a conditional judgement.
requirements.adequate_response: Argument for, argument against, identifies OC (not cash price), applies a stated priority, conditional judgement.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 (b) 7 marks Ap/An: implications - limited resources, reallocate; 2020 P2 Q4(c) application; 2023 P1 Q1. No ER misconception beyond defining OC.
requirements.gap: Change-of-constraint case (OC disappears when resources expand) - J-P03 idea.
requirements.repetition: Sand River case reused in J-006, J-P02, J-P03; V uses six different scenarios.
requirements.why: V cases have real trade-offs; J's stem supplies the ranking so the judgement is forced.

requirements.syllabus_text: describe the factors of production (land, labour, capital, entrepreneurship)
requirements.demand: Recall and apply: define, classify a given input/person, distinguish money from capital and supervision from entrepreneurship.
requirements.adequate_response: Correct factor for each input with the reason; entrepreneur = organising + risk; capital = produced equipment, not cash.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P2 Q4(a) identify and give examples of three factors from the extract [6] (ER: majority identified and linked to extract; entrepreneur among answers); 2022 P1 Q2 supervisors = labour (ER: a few gave entrepreneurship); 2023 P1 Q3 shop assistant = labour (well answered).
requirements.gap: No single task asking learner to identify and exemplify all four factors from an extract (2020 P2 Q4(a)).
requirements.repetition: Four DEFs duplicated across banks (V-010..013 = J-002/004/006/008); V-P02 repeats them.
requirements.why: V: precise defs plus both exam-evidenced misconceptions. J: contextual identification cards (after marking fix).

requirements.syllabus_text: explain allocation of resources in market, planned and mixed economic systems
requirements.demand: Understand/analyse: explain how each system allocates (who decides, through what mechanism, who owns resources).
requirements.adequate_response: Market: private ownership, price signals, profit motive; planned/command: state plan and (usually) state ownership; mixed: both. Can answer what/how/for whom.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q3 who owns resources in a market economy (ER: some omitted 'private'); 2021 P2 Q2(a) features of command economy [6] (govt owns factors, planned production); 2023 P1 Q2 price control under command->market (poorly answered); 2023 P2 Q25(a) command economy features (ER: some gave features of command economy); 2024 P2 Q4(a) name two other systems (command/planned, market) (ER p.1 line ~746). Exam uses 'command'; syllabus says 'planned'.
requirements.gap: Command-economy synonym and features (state ownership, planned output, price control, limited choice); market features (private ownership, price mechanism, profit, competition); what/how/for whom in each; real-country examples (Namibia = mixed).
requirements.repetition: V-005/J-010, V-006/J-016, V-004... heavy 1:1 overlaps; J water case reused 5 times.
requirements.why: J mechanism cards explain allocation; V definitions add what/how/for whom and the private/state ownership (after revision).

requirements.syllabus_text: evaluate the merits and effectiveness of different economic systems
requirements.demand: Evaluate: judge each system against an objective, with conditions.
requirements.adequate_response: Merits and limits of market, planned and mixed systems with a supported conclusion; e.g. why a country might change systems.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q2(b) comment on effectiveness of command system [7] (ER: both positive and negative; fairly well answered); 2021 P2 Q2(c) evaluate merits of changing command -> mixed [7] (ER: poorly answered; most could not give advantages of mixed system); 2024 P2 Q4 reasons countries move away from market system (ER lines ~746-790).
requirements.gap: Generic merits/limits of market, planned and mixed systems (V notes list them; no card tests them); 'evaluate changing from system X to system Y' item focusing on advantages of a mixed system.
requirements.repetition: V-009/J-017/V-P01/J-P02 all use the same water/transport access case.
requirements.why: V-P04 and J-P03 give different evaluation contrasts; J-017 and J-P02 have clean stems.

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the meaning of specialisation and the division of labour
requirements.demand: Understand: define each, distinguish them, link (DoL leads to specialisation), give examples.
requirements.adequate_response: Division of labour: process split into tasks; specialisation: workers/areas concentrate on a narrower activity; applies to an extract.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 Q1(a) describe how DoL leads to specialisation with extract examples [4] (ER: learners described instead of specifying concepts; capped at 2 marks; examples from thatch-grass extract). 2022 ER mark scheme definitions.
requirements.gap: None; combine J-002 with V-001/V-003. Optional: extract-based 'describe how DoL leads to specialisation' item.
requirements.repetition: V-P02, J-P01 are bundles of cards.
requirements.why: V lacks a plain definition of specialisation; J lacks nothing but duplicates V-001.

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse the advantages and disadvantages of specialisation and the division of labour
requirements.demand: Analyse: explain mechanisms (practice, switching, scale) and risks (boredom, interdependence, skill loss, immobility).
requirements.adequate_response: Mechanism chains for advantages and disadvantages for firm/worker/country with conditions.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q4 list three disadvantages of DoL [3] (well answered: boredom, immobility, dependency, loss of skills, lack of variety); 2024 P1 Q3 explain why loss of job satisfaction is a disadvantage [2] (boredom, low quality, low output); 2023 P2(d) both sides for a country (ER: learners wrote about individuals, not the country).
requirements.gap: Stand-alone disadvantages cards (boredom -> lower quality/absence; loss of skills; difficulty changing jobs; interdependence/strikes; less variety); advantages beyond practice/switching (economies of scale, lower unit cost, higher wages/quality).
requirements.repetition: Practice/switching mechanism appears in V-005, J-006, J-009, V-P01(b), J-P02(b).
requirements.why: V: dependence and numerate case; J: bottleneck and individual evaluation; boredom handled only inside evaluations.

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss the various levels of specialisation (individual, regional, national)
requirements.demand: Understand/evaluate: identify level, distinguish levels, discuss gains and risks at each level.
requirements.adequate_response: Correct level for a case; keeps national export dependence separate from worker boredom; judgement with conditions.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P1 Q3 list two levels [2] (international/national, regional, industries, workers/individuals); 2023 P2(d) discuss whether only benefits if a country specialises in coffee [7] (ER: wrote about individuals; no link to extract).
requirements.repetition: Regional evaluation appears in J-012, J-P02, J-P03, V-P03; national in J-014, V-P04.
requirements.why: V: definitions, level-confusion, extended; J: level-specific mechanism and evaluation flashcards.

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the differences between the private and public sector
requirements.demand: Understand: contrast ownership, aim, finance, goods/services provided; do not confuse with activity or 'public company'.
requirements.adequate_response: Private: owned/controlled/funded by individuals, profit aim; public: government-owned, essential services, funded by taxation.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2024 P2 'Outline the differences between public and private sector' (ER: majority scored 3; private = owned/controlled/funded by private individuals + profit; public = government owned, essential goods/services, taxation); 2024 P2 (d) education private or public; 2020 P2 (d) justify why water not left to private sector [7]; 2021 P1 Q24 MTC.
requirements.gap: Aim, finance and control differences (taught in V notes, tested by no card in either bank); 'why a service might be kept in the public sector' reasoning.
requirements.repetition: Ownership-vs-activity lesson repeated in V-003, V-018, J-002, J-022.
requirements.why: V-002 for the 'public' trap; J-001 once revised for the two-sided contrast.

requirements.syllabus_text: describe the different forms of business organisations: sole proprietors, partnerships, private companies, public companies, multi-nationals, co-operatives, close corporations, public corporations
requirements.demand: Recall/understand: define and identify the eight forms from features; know limited/unlimited liability.
requirements.adequate_response: Accurate features per form incl. liability, ownership, share availability, state ownership, countries of operation.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q5 partnership: 2 people, not more than 20 (ER: 'members' not accepted); 2021 P1 Q4 limited liability of close corporation; Q6 two types of co-operatives; Q24 public corporation -> public limited company; 2022 P1 Q3 identify form (two friends, half shares each, limited liability = private limited company) and Q4 multinational not always private limited [False]; 2024 P1 Q4 reasons sole proprietor converts to CC (limited liability, continuity, tax, more capital).
requirements.gap: Identify a form from case facts (2022 Q3); types of co-operative (2021 Q6); public corporation -> public limited company (2021 Q24).
requirements.repetition: V-P02 repeats the eight DEFs; J has a DEF and a FEATURE for each form, several answered from the stem.
requirements.why: V defs are complete and examinable; J features are stem-restating and omit limited liability.

requirements.syllabus_text: compare and choose the most appropriate form of business
requirements.demand: Evaluate: choose a form given finance, control, risk, continuity.
requirements.adequate_response: Advantages and disadvantages of the relevant forms applied to the case; conditional recommendation.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 advantages/disadvantages of becoming a public limited company [8, both-sided]; 2022 P2 (c) [6] (ER: learners gave advantages of sole trader instead of answering the question); 2023 P2 (c) benefit of staying small [7] (ER: advantages of sole trader, not advantages/disadvantages of staying small); 2024 P1 Q4 ER: disadvantages of sole proprietor without reference to sole proprietorship.
requirements.gap: Recall cards for advantages/disadvantages of each form; 'why convert sole proprietor to close corporation/company' (2024); privatisation / listing (2021).
requirements.repetition: Copper Acacia case used in J-020, J-P02, J-P03.
requirements.why: V has five different cases and the notes' advantage/disadvantage lists; J-020 is the single strong J item.

requirements.syllabus_text: define a trade union
requirements.demand: Recall + precision
requirements.adequate_response: State: organisation of workers that represents them in dealings with employers (about pay and conditions, through collective bargaining)
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q3(a) define + two types (4 marks; ER: well answered, 'workers' organisation represents workers in dealings with management and owners'); syllabus glossary line 897 adds 'collective bargaining'. 2020 P1 Q7 and 2024 P1 Q5 ask collective bargaining; ER 2020: learners treat bargaining as the union.
requirements.why: V-001 awards 2 marks like the exam; no standalone card defines collective bargaining (syllabus glossary names it).

requirements.syllabus_text: identify the aims of trade unions
requirements.demand: Recall/identify
requirements.adequate_response: Name aims: higher pay, better/safer conditions, hours, job security, fair treatment, training
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 Q4 stem (retrenchment); 2023 P1 Q16 wage rise -> cost-push inflation (link). No direct 'identify aims' question 2020-2024.
requirements.gap: Neither bank has a card on higher wages as a union aim or on hours/fair treatment
requirements.repetition: V-005 duplicates J-003 and is cued
requirements.why: J-003 open recall + V-006 application + revised V-004; add pay/hours card

requirements.syllabus_text: describe the advantages of joining a trade union
requirements.demand: Describe (give reason + consequence) with several distinct benefits
requirements.adequate_response: Give distinct benefits: negotiated pay/conditions, representation in grievances/disciplinary, legal advice, protection from unfair dismissal, training, welfare/strike pay
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 Q4(a) 'List six benefits to a worker of joining a trade union' (breadth demand, 2022); 2021 P2 Q3(d) wellbeing (unions: negotiate, training, counselling, benefits).
requirements.gap: Both cover only collective voice / grievance help. No card gives legal advice, dismissal protection, training/welfare benefits that the exam asks six of (V notes list them; no card tests them)
requirements.why: Depth from J-004 and V-009; breadth missing in both

requirements.syllabus_text: describe the types of trade unions in Namibia (e.g. white collar, blue collar, craft unions)
requirements.demand: Recall + describe/classify
requirements.adequate_response: Name/define at least white collar, blue collar, craft; recognise general and industrial union also accepted
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q3(a): craft, general, industrial/blue collar, white collar accepted; 2022 P1 Q5 name two types (ER: learners gave names of unions); 2022 P1 ER lists general, industrial, white collar.
requirements.gap: General and industrial unions not covered by either bank; J lacks 2-mark definitions; no named-Namibian-union content (not required by bullet)
requirements.why: V has 2-mark defs plus classification traps; J name-two item needs rewording

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss the factors affecting trade union activities in Namibia
requirements.demand: Analyse/discuss factors
requirements.adequate_response: Link membership/participation, scarcity of skills, demand for output, available labour, employer finances, to bargaining strength
requirements.exam_evidence: No direct 2020-2024 question on factors; 2023 P1 Q16 link wage rise to cost-push inflation. Namibia-specific legal framework not examined in these papers.
requirements.gap: No card on membership size/participation (V notes) or legal/government framework; no wage-push-inflation link
requirements.why: Similar quality; J-P03 contrast design is best transfer test

requirements.syllabus_text: explain and evaluate the role of trade unions
requirements.demand: Explain then evaluate (for/against/judgement)
requirements.adequate_response: Benefits and costs of union action for workers, firms; conditional judgement
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q3(b),(d) dispute resolution (negotiate, conciliation, arbitration, labour court) and wellbeing; 2022 P2 Q4; 2020 P1 Q7 collective bargaining meaning.
requirements.gap: Neither bank tests dispute resolution (conciliation/arbitration/labour court) examined 2021 (6 marks); no wage-push inflation link
requirements.repetition: V-018 and V-P04 both evaluate union formation
requirements.why: V supplies employer-side benefit/limitation and industrial action; J supplies clearer bargaining-vs-union item

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the role of employer association
requirements.demand: Explain roles; distinguish from union
requirements.adequate_response: State what an association is and 2+ roles (negotiate with unions for members, advise on labour law, training, lobby government, bulk buying)
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q6 'Name two roles of an employer association' (ER: learners gave union roles); 2021 P2 Q3(c) describe employers' association (ER: poorly answered, confused with employee associations); 2021 Q3(d).
requirements.gap: Neither lists role set (lobbying, labour-law advice, bulk buying) as exam wants
requirements.why: V has definition + misconception cards; J-016 adds training role

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the need for exchange
requirements.demand: Explain cause-effect (specialisation -> need to exchange; barter failure)
requirements.adequate_response: Link specialisation to exchange; barter and double coincidence of wants
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P1 mark scheme for market mentions 'money/barter'; no direct 2020-2024 question on need for exchange found.
requirements.why: V barter definition + J money-solves-barter chain

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the functions, quality and types of money
requirements.demand: Define, classify, apply (function vs quality vs type)
requirements.adequate_response: Name/define functions (medium of exchange, unit of account/measure of value, store of value, deferred payment), qualities (durability, portability, divisibility, acceptability, scarcity, homogeneity) and types (cash, deposits, electronic)
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q9 measure of value; 2022 Q7 unit of account (ER: learners said store of value); 2023 Q8 medium of exchange (well answered); 2024 Q6 homogeneity (ER: learners said 'same value', scheme: same units + hard to counterfeit).
requirements.gap: J lacks cards on scarcity, homogeneity, store of value, deferred payment, cash and deposits
requirements.why: V has a card per function/quality/type incl. homogeneity (2024 Q6) plus the unit-vs-store error; J has better chained applications

requirements.syllabus_text: define and calculate exchange rate
requirements.demand: Define; apply multiplication/division; interpret direction
requirements.adequate_response: Define exchange rate; compute N$ cost = foreign amount x rate; interpret change
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 Q20, 2022 Q6 define (ER: must say price/value of one currency in terms of another); 2024 Q17 US$30 000 x N$17,80 = N$534 000 (2 marks, N$ must be shown); 2021 Q19 define trade.
requirements.gap: Neither asks 'how many foreign units for N$x' in a 2-mark form except V-010; J only multiplication
requirements.why: V definition/interpretation/division; J-012 as exam-form calculation (with peg line removed)

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss the effects of fluctuating exchange rates on the economy
requirements.demand: Analyse and evaluate effects (imports, exports, firms, households)
requirements.adequate_response: Depreciation: imports dearer, exports cheaper/competitive, possible inflation; appreciation reverse; conditions
requirements.exam_evidence: 2023 P2: define depreciation (ER: confused with forex), evaluate depreciation (7 marks, ER: learners one-sided); 2021 Q13 effect of interest rate on exchange rate; 2020 P1 Q21 causes of fluctuating rates; 2024 P2 depreciation/competitiveness stems.
requirements.gap: Neither covers broader macro effects (inflation, balance of trade, employment, tourism) nor causes of fluctuation (2020 Q21); V lacks exporter-competitiveness evaluation, J lacks depreciation definition and appreciation
requirements.why: V definition and firm/household effects; J-014 (revised) evaluation

requirements.syllabus_text: describe and evaluate the functions of central banks, stock exchanges and commercial banks
requirements.demand: Describe functions; distinguish institutions; evaluate
requirements.adequate_response: Define each institution; list central bank functions (issue notes, banker to government and banks, lender of last resort, monetary policy, supervision); stock exchange role (raise capital, trade securities); commercial bank services (deposits, payments, loans)
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q (c) functions of the Namibian Stock Exchange and effect on economy (8 marks); 2023 P1 Q6 why PLC lists shares; Q7 two central bank functions (ER: learners listed commercial-bank functions); 2024 P1 Q7 define stock exchange (ER: learners defined market/exchange rate); 2024 P2 Q23(a) describe functions of central bank (6 marks, 'list not describe'); 2020 P2 central bank and inflation.
requirements.gap: V lacks a stock-exchange evaluation and government-securities function (2021); J lacks definitions of the three institutions, lender of last resort, supervision, and stock-exchange role beyond equity
requirements.repetition: Repeated loan-vs-repayment reasoning across V-016, V-P03(d), J-018, J-P02(c), J-P03
requirements.why: V has per-institution definitions, functions and misconception; J supplies exam-shaped evaluations

requirements.syllabus_text: explain a market
requirements.demand: Define + explain
requirements.adequate_response: State that a market brings buyers and sellers together to exchange goods, services or resources (not necessarily one place)
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P1 Q8 'Outline the meaning of a market' (2 marks; ER: well answered: place where buyers and sellers come together to negotiate price/exchange goods and services for money/barter). No other 2020-2024 item on the bullet found.
requirements.gap: Neither card links market to price determination/negotiation of price (in the 2022 scheme)
requirements.why: 2-mark definition and application card

requirements.syllabus_text: explain different types of markets
requirements.demand: Classify markets by a stated basis
requirements.adequate_response: Classify given case by type of market
requirements.exam_evidence: No 2020-2024 question on types of markets found; the syllabus does not say which types (UNRESOLVED: local/national/international, product/factor/financial, physical/digital?).
requirements.gap: Syllabus does not define 'types'. V covers only physical/digital; J only product/factor. Local/national/international and financial/commodity types (in V notes) have no card
requirements.why: Different interpretations; neither covers geographic or financial markets

requirements.syllabus_text: define and illustrate demand and supply
requirements.demand: Recall definitions; apply plotting of schedules and distinguish movement from shift
requirements.adequate_response: Defines demand/supply (willing and able, price, period, ceteris paribus); plots D and S from a schedule with labelled axes, units and origin; shows own-price movement along both curves
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 gen. comments (diagrams, arrows for shifts); 2022 P1 Q9-10; 2023 P2 Q4(b); 2024 P1 Q9. ER 2022: learners could not label and show equilibrium. Glossary L744, L880
requirements.repetition: J-001/003/005 restate definitions already scored in V-020/021; V-003/004 overlap partly
requirements.why: V has verified diagram cards and two-mark definitions; J definitions duplicate V with undivided marks

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss and illustrate the principle of equilibrium price
requirements.demand: Apply: locate equilibrium on schedule/diagram; interpret excess demand/supply and price adjustment
requirements.adequate_response: Equilibrium where Qd=Qs; shows E with projections; at higher/lower price states excess supply/demand with magnitude; price pressure and movements along unchanged curves
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 ER: show equilibrium point and label; 2024 P2 Q(c) price fixed below equilibrium (shortage). Glossary L784
requirements.why: V-006 diagram + J-007 excess-supply card + J-018 price-control bridge; drop V-007/V-008

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse simple market situations with changes in supply and demand
requirements.demand: Apply/analyse: draw and read shifts; separate shift from movement; locate new equilibrium
requirements.adequate_response: Shows D or S shift with arrows, original and new equilibrium, direction of price and quantity; states other curve unchanged
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q8 (advertising plus technology), 2021 P2 diagram (supply decrease), 2022 P1 Q10, 2022 P1 hair stylists (fall in demand), 2024 P1 (c) uranium demand increase
requirements.gap: No demand-decrease diagram or simultaneous D and S shift diagram in either bank
requirements.why: V diagrams verified; J-015 gives supply decrease (needs image); both miss demand decrease

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss the causes of changes in demand and supply conditions
requirements.demand: Understand/apply: name determinants with direction and explain the channel
requirements.adequate_response: Lists factors with increase/decrease (income normal/inferior, substitutes/complements, tastes/advertising, population; costs, technology, weather, taxes/subsidies); explains why curve shifts at given prices
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q24(a) three supply factors; 2023 P2 Q6(b) four demand factors (ER: must indicate rise/fall; confused with PED factors); 2023 P1 Q9; 2022 P1 Q14 ER brand/category
requirements.gap: No complement, inferior-good, tax/subsidy, population or expectations items (V notes teach them)
requirements.why: V misconception cards are exam-evidenced; J adds income mechanism and ceteris-paribus phrasing

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse such changes to show effects on price
requirements.demand: Analyse: derive direction of price and quantity for each shift and combinations
requirements.adequate_response: States effect on equilibrium price and quantity for each single shift and why combined shifts are indeterminate without magnitude
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q8; 2022 P1 Q10; 2021 P2 ER: new equilibrium price higher, quantity lower on supply decrease
requirements.why: V-017 + V-018 + V-019 plus J-015 for supply decrease

requirements.syllabus_text: define price elasticity of demand and supply
requirements.demand: Recall definition and formula; distinguish quantity demanded from quantity supplied
requirements.adequate_response: PED and PES = %change quantity / %change price; ratio not percentage; classify elastic/inelastic/perfectly inelastic
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 Q18 ER (definition not formula); 2021 P1 Q9 (define perfectly inelastic: poorly answered); 2022 Q11; 2023 P1 Q11; 2023 P2 Q6(a) ER (wrong formula, QS vs QD); glossary L850, L853
requirements.gap: No define-perfectly-inelastic card; formula card needed
requirements.why: V-009/010 two-mark split; add J-001 revised formula card

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss and apply price elasticity of demand and supply
requirements.demand: Apply/discuss: use coefficient for revenue and pricing decisions; explain determinants
requirements.adequate_response: Predicts effect of price change on total revenue by elasticity; explains substitutes, necessity, proportion of income, time, spare capacity; revenue is not profit
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P1 Q25(b),(c) price discrimination from PED; 2024 P1 Q10 (two reasons luxury holiday elastic); 2024 P2 Q(b) maize meal elastic or inelastic; 2023 P2
requirements.gap: No determinants-of-PED card (substitutes, necessity, % of income, time); no elastic-demand price-cut revenue card
requirements.why: J-005/J-007 for mechanisms; V-P cards for extended work

requirements.syllabus_text: perform simple calculations of elasticity and inelasticity of demand and supply
requirements.demand: Apply: calculate %changes and the coefficient; classify; interpret
requirements.adequate_response: Computes %change quantity and price from initial values, divides, gives coefficient without % sign, classifies correctly
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q24(b) PES calc; 2021 P1 Q25(a) PED calc 5 marks (formula, each %, ratio; ER: % sign lost marks); 2022 Q11; 2023 P2 Q6(a)
requirements.gap: Percentages-given calc (2021), falling-price case, and sign convention card missing
requirements.why: pair V and J calcs (elastic and inelastic; PED and PES) with 2-mark working/result marking

requirements.syllabus_text: define advertising
requirements.demand: Recall definition
requirements.adequate_response: Paid communication aimed at informing or persuading potential buyers about a product/service/organisation
requirements.exam_evidence: No 2020-24 'define advertising' item found; 2023 P2 Q4(a) reasons for advertising
requirements.gap: Definition not tested in exams; do not over-weight
requirements.why: J-001 definition is more precise (paid)

requirements.syllabus_text: describe the purpose and methods of advertising
requirements.demand: Understand/describe: list purposes and methods; match method to audience
requirements.adequate_response: Names reasons (inform, persuade, increase sales/market share, brand image/loyalty, compete) and methods (TV, radio, newspapers, posters/billboards, leaflets, internet/social media, exhibitions); links method to audience
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q11 (3 methods, well answered); 2023 P2 Q4(a) (six reasons; ER: forms confused with reasons); 2023 P2 Q4(b) and 2024 P1 Q9 and 2020 P1 Q8 (advertising shifts demand); 2021 P1 Q25(c) non-price competition
requirements.gap: No methods list card, no reasons list, no advertising-shifts-demand diagram card
requirements.why: V has more coverage but needs list cards and demand-shift link

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss and evaluate pricing and output policies in perfect competition and monopoly
requirements.demand: Discuss/evaluate: compare price taker vs maker, output decisions, consumer outcomes
requirements.adequate_response: Defines both models, price taker vs price maker, demand constraint on monopoly, scale savings vs pass-through; judgement conditional on outcomes
requirements.exam_evidence: 2023 P1 Q12 (competitive vs monopoly prices; price taker/maker); 2021 P1 Q16 (why government controls monopolies); 2021 P1 Q25(b) price discrimination; glossary L827, L862 (MR, profit maximisation MC=MR)
requirements.gap: Price maker term, price discrimination, non-price competition and (optional) MC=MR output rule untested as flashcards
requirements.why: V for definitions and constraints; J for cost-vs-price comparison (after data fix)

requirements.syllabus_text: differentiate between and discuss wage and non-wage factors affecting an individual’s choice of occupation
requirements.demand: Understand/apply/discuss: classify factors and weigh them for a person
requirements.adequate_response: Defines wage vs non-wage, classifies examples (pay, overtime, bonus; hours, safety, security, fringe benefits, training, location, job satisfaction), compares offers on a common basis and gives a conditional choice
requirements.exam_evidence: 2024 P1 Q11 (two non-wage factors; ER well answered; list incl. natural ability, access to education, training, finance, fringe benefits, security); 2024 earnings ER (overtime, bonus)
requirements.gap: Non-wage list card (fringe benefits, security, education/finance access) missing
requirements.why: V definitions and open evaluation; J-004 for net-pay calculation

requirements.syllabus_text: not printed in syllabus.txt (grep for 'mobil' returns nothing)
requirements.demand: Define and distinguish occupational and geographical mobility
requirements.adequate_response: Occupational mobility = ability to switch between different occupations; geographical = move between areas
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P1 Q12 (ER: confused with geographical mobility and occupational immobility); 2024 P1 earnings answer 'geographical immobility'
requirements.gap: Exam entitlement beyond printed bullets; keep separate from entitlement
requirements.why: only V covers it

requirements.syllabus_text: identify and analyse the factors determining earnings
requirements.demand: Analyse: link demand for and supply of a type of labour (orders, productivity, training time, hours, bargaining) to pay.
requirements.adequate_response: Name factors and trace demand/supply (or hours x rate) to a pay outcome using stated conditions.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q19 (3 marks) 'equally qualified nurses... different income'; ER: learners gave general reasons, did not link; 2022 P1 (d) 8 marks 'Justify why differences in earnings in different occupations' (ER lists compensating differentials, skill demand, productivity, unions, certification, location, natural ability); 2024 P2 (c) 'same skills, different wage rates'; 2020 P2 Q1 minimum wage diagram.
requirements.gap: Neither bank has cards on trade unions/bargaining, legal minimum wage, compensating differentials (risk/unsocial hours), seniority/experience/responsibility, or within-skill pay differences, all of which the exam rewards. J has no labour-market diagram.
requirements.repetition: Hours x rate and scarce-skill chain repeated: V-003/V-006/J-002/J-005; J-001/007/012/015.
requirements.why: V supplies the only correct labour-market diagram and less scaffolded chains; J supplies mechanism cards but with restated-prompt marks.

requirements.syllabus_text: describe and explain the differences in earnings between different occupational groups and different economic sectors (male/female; skilled/unskilled; private/public; agricultural/manufacturing/ services)
requirements.demand: Describe and explain (understand/apply): explain a stated difference using group data without over-claiming causation.
requirements.adequate_response: Distinguish averages from individuals and group composition; give a mechanism for each pairing (gender, skill, ownership sector, agriculture/manufacturing/services).
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q19 ER lists seniority, private (higher)/public (lower), regional, bonus/overtime, experience, responsibility; 2022 P1 (d) as above; 2022 P1 Q (c) women self-employment/gender wage inequality extract.
requirements.gap: No card on within-occupation pay differences (seniority, experience, location, bonus). Public sector pay claims are unverified.
requirements.repetition: J scarce-skill mechanism repeated across sector labels (J-007, J-012, J-015).
requirements.why: J pairs each printed grouping (male/female, skilled, private/public, agriculture, manufacturing, service) with a mechanism card; V mostly defines terms (013-016).

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse and discuss changes in earnings over time between occupations and between economic sectors
requirements.demand: Analyse/discuss: explain why relative earnings change and interpret nominal v real change.
requirements.adequate_response: Use demand/supply changes, productivity, bargaining; compute real change from a price index; avoid single-cause claims.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q10 define real income (ER: most defined disposable income); 2022 P1 Q13 real disposable income N$5,000 at 3.5% inflation = N$4,825; 2023 P2 real income per capita (ER: only 1 mark).
requirements.gap: No card defines real income; no card gives the exam's real income method (income minus inflation% x income = N$4,825 vs exact deflation N$4,831); no occupational/sector time-series data card.
requirements.why: V gives nominal/real vocabulary and exam-evidenced misconception; J gives growth-gap mechanism (J-017) and supply-response (J-016).

requirements.syllabus_text: explain economic rent and transfer earnings
requirements.demand: Explain/apply: separate reward into minimum and excess and use a stated figure.
requirements.adequate_response: Define both, split a stated reward, and avoid reversing them; optional diagram (area between supply curve and wage).
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 4(b) 7 marks soccer player N$1,000 willing N$800: TE N$800, rent N$200; ER 'Poorly answered. Majority lack subject knowledge'; graph optional (+2).
requirements.gap: No diagram card showing rent as the area between wage and supply curve.
requirements.why: Definitions V-017/018, distinction and numeric split J-019/020, reversal MISCON V-020.

requirements.syllabus_text: describe how and why different income groups have different expenditure patterns (spending, saving, borrowing)
requirements.demand: Describe and explain (understand/apply): compare amounts and shares for different incomes and give reasons.
requirements.adequate_response: Use share = spending/income; explain why low-income households spend more of income on essentials, save less, borrow for emergencies with limited access.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P2 (d) 'savings and spending patterns change for different groups and income levels over a career'; 2022 P2 (c) factors determining spending.
requirements.gap: No card on factors determining spending (disposable income, wealth, expectations) or life-cycle pattern.
requirements.why: J gives the why for spending, saving and borrowing; V mostly defines.

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse the different motives for spending, saving and borrowing
requirements.demand: Analyse: identify and develop motives for each of the three behaviours.
requirements.adequate_response: Name spending motives (necessity, want), saving motives (emergency, planned purchase, interest), borrowing motives (bridge, urgent need).
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 (c) factors for spending of a soccer player; 2023 P2 (b) interest rate fall on savings of different individuals.
requirements.gap: No want-driven spending motive card (status, advertising); no retirement/education saving motive card.
requirements.why: J has separate motive cards for all three; V has only precautionary saving and one borrowing card.

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse and discuss changes in patterns of expenditure between groups and over a period of time
requirements.demand: Analyse/discuss: explain how price, interest, income changes alter patterns.
requirements.adequate_response: Compare shares over time, effect of price rises on fixed income, interest effects on saving and borrowing, group differences in response.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P2 (d) career pattern; 2023 P2 (b) interest rates; 2022 P2 (c) inflation, interest, taxes on spending.
requirements.gap: No card on inflation effect on spending/saving; no life-cycle card; no tax or credit availability changes.
requirements.why: V-009 time-share; J-016/017 price and interest responses.

requirements.syllabus_text: describe and analyse the principle of profit maximisation as a goal
requirements.demand: Describe/analyse: define; distinguish highest profit from highest revenue/output; apply TR-TC and MC=MR.
requirements.adequate_response: State profit = TR-TC; maximum where MC = MR; compare options by profit not revenue.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q4(a) 3 marks describe profit maximisation (MC = MR; TR-TC); 2022 P2 3(c) 7 marks 'whether a firm should always maximise profit' (ER: majority scored 1 mark stating MR = MC; ER notes 'could not give the difference between TC and TR'); 2023 P2 Q2(a) link productivity/maximum profits (6).
requirements.gap: Neither bank has an MR/MC table card; J never states MC = MR; V states it only in the definition. No card on goals other than profit (2022 P2 3(c)).
requirements.repetition: J uses the same 10/20/30 batch data in J-001, J-008, J-P01.
requirements.why: V-001 (revised) states the rule; J-008/J-P01 provide the misconception and the calculation.

requirements.syllabus_text: define production
requirements.demand: Define: goods and services created to satisfy wants.
requirements.adequate_response: Definition including services.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P2 Q4(b) production v productivity (ER: learners did not mention goods/services).
requirements.why: V-004 is more complete and marked at 2.

requirements.syllabus_text: describe what determines the demand for factors of production
requirements.demand: Describe: derived demand; contribution (productivity); price of factor and of substitutes/complements.
requirements.adequate_response: Explain demand for labour/capital as derived from product demand and productivity.
requirements.exam_evidence: No direct item found; 2022 P1 Q15 productivity of capital goods (ER: poorly answered, learners did not define capital goods).
requirements.gap: No card on factor price changes, relative factor prices, marginal revenue product (V notes mention MRP; no card), or capital goods definition.
requirements.why: V definition/chain plus J-005 complementarity.

requirements.syllabus_text: analyse particular situations to show the effects of substituting one factor for another
requirements.demand: Analyse: compare factor combinations for cost, output and employment.
requirements.adequate_response: Compute profit under alternative methods, note full costs, utilisation, effects on workers.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P2 and 2022 ER mention machinery/capital intensity; 2022 P1 Q15 'Some learners described capital intensive'.
requirements.gap: No card on a change in relative factor price causing substitution; no capital-/labour-intensive definition card.
requirements.why: J quantifies; V states benefit/limit qualitatively.

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the meaning of productivity
requirements.demand: Explain/understand: output per unit of input; differ from production.
requirements.adequate_response: Give formula and distinguish production from productivity.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q13 formula (2); 2021 P2 Q4(b) production v productivity (ER: fairly well answered, mentioned output measured against input); 2022 P1 Q15 productivity of capital goods (3).
requirements.why: V-001 definition with J-011 misconception.

requirements.syllabus_text: show how productivity is measured
requirements.demand: Apply/calculate: output divided by input.
requirements.adequate_response: Calculate and interpret productivity from figures.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q13 write the formula (2); 2022 P1 Q15 output per hour.
requirements.why: J-003 marks formula and result; V-006 adds percentage interpretation.

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss how productivity can be improved
requirements.demand: Discuss: weigh methods (training, equipment, layout, incentives).
requirements.adequate_response: Explain two or more methods and the mechanism for each.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2020 P1 Q14 list two ways (1 mark); 2021 P2 Q4(c) 7 marks 'how a company might improve production' (training, better machines, combine factors, division of labour, participation, profit sharing; ER: learners listed without explaining).
requirements.gap: No card on machinery/technology, motivation/incentive (profit sharing, piece rate), division of labour, health/education as ways to raise productivity.
requirements.why: V-009 and V-010 plus J-006 bottleneck.

requirements.syllabus_text: explain the effect of Information Technology on productivity
requirements.demand: Explain: IT effects with conditions.
requirements.adequate_response: Give mechanism and a risk (training, downtime).
requirements.exam_evidence: No IT-specific past-paper question found in extracts.
requirements.why: V cards require the learner to supply conditions.

requirements.syllabus_text: discuss the effects of HIV and AIDS on productivity
requirements.demand: Discuss: link illness/absence/stigma to output and cost, without status inference.
requirements.adequate_response: State effects (absenteeism, lower output, higher costs, reduced labour supply, discrimination) and note support/treatment.
requirements.exam_evidence: 2021 P1 Q14 ways to protect workers with HIV/AIDS; 2022 P1 Q16 two disadvantages (ER: absenteeism, low productivity, increased costs, reduced supply of labour, discrimination); 2023 P2 Q2(b) negative influence on productivity and profit (6).
requirements.gap: Neither bank states the exam's disadvantages list or worker-protection measures; J-010 is mistagged.
requirements.why: V states the definition and exam-aligned absence effect; J-009/J-010 over-scaffolded.

requirements.syllabus_text: define total, average, fixed and variable costs
requirements.demand: Recall plus classification and calculation
requirements.adequate_response: Define each term; classify; compute AC and AFC
requirements.exam_evidence: 2022 P1 Q17 AFC; Q18 variable cost; 2023 P1 Q14 fixed cost 150; 2023 P2 (c); 2021 P2 (d)
